'''Robert Allan Ridley Parker''' (born December 14, 1936) is an American [[physicist]] and [[astronomer]], former director of the [[NASA]] Management Office at the [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]], and a retired [[NASA]] [[astronaut]]. He was a [[mission specialist]] on two [[Space Shuttle]] missions, [[STS-9]] and [[STS-35]].

He has logged over 3,500 hours flying time in [[jet aircraft]] and 463 hours in space.<ref name="nasabio" />

==Biography==
===Early life===
Parker was born December 14, 1936, in [[New York City]], but grew up in [[Shrewsbury, Massachusetts|Shrewsbury]], [[Massachusetts]]. He attended primary and secondary schools in Shrewsbury. He received a [[Bachelor of Arts|BA]] in [[astronomy]] and [[physics]] from [[Amherst College]] in 1958 and a [[PhD]] in astronomy from the [[California Institute of Technology]] in 1962. His doctoral dissertation, ''The physical conditions pertaining to some possible supernova remnants'', was supervised by [[Guido Münch]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://astrogen.aas.org/front/searchdetails.php?agnumber=2585|title=Robert Allan Ridley Parker|work=AstroGen|publisher=American Astronomical Society|access-date=2022-12-19}}</ref> Prior to his selection for astronaut training, Parker was an [[associate professor]] of astronomy at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]].<ref name="nasabio">{{cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/parker_robert.pdf|title=Robert Parker NASA Biography|publisher=NASA|access-date=May 14, 2021 |date=December 2005}}</ref>

===NASA career===
[[File:S035 Parker.jpg|thumb|left|200px|Parker points instruments on ASTRO-1 on ''Columbia'''s aft flight deck during STS-35]]
Parker was selected as a scientist-astronaut by [[NASA]] in August 1967.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/30779535/muncie_evening_press/|title=New Citizens to be Astros|newspaper=Muncie Evening Press|location=Muncie, Indiana|date=August 3, 1967|page=19|via=Newspapers.com|agency=UPI}}</ref> He was a member of the Astronaut Support Crews for the [[Apollo 15]] and [[Apollo 17|17]] missions, and was the person to whom the final words spoken by a man standing on the surface of the Moon ([[Gene Cernan]]) were addressed.  Later, he served as program scientist for the [[Skylab]] Program Director's Office during the three crewed Skylab flights.<ref name="nasabio" />

From March 1988 to March 1989, Parker was stationed at [[NASA Headquarters]] in [[Washington, D.C.]], where he served as director of the Space Flight/Space Station Integration Office.<ref name="nasabio" />

A veteran of two [[Spacelab]] missions, Parker was a [[mission specialist]] on [[STS-9]]/Spacelab-1 (November 28–December 8, 1983) and on [[STS-35]] (December 2–10, 1990), which featured the [[ASTRO-1]] ultraviolet astronomy laboratory.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/shuttle/shuttlemissions/archives/sts-9.html|title=STS-9|publisher=NASA|access-date=January 4, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-35/mission-sts-35.html|title=STS-35|publisher=NASA|access-date=January 4, 2018|archive-date=December 1, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201101822/http://science.ksc.nasa.gov/shuttle/missions/sts-35/mission-sts-35.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

===Post-NASA career===
Parker was director of the Division of Policy and Plans for the Office of Space Flight at NASA Headquarters from January 1991 to December 1991. From January 1992 to November 1993, he was director of the Spacelab and Operations Program. From December 1993 to August 1997 he was manager of the Space Operations Utilization Program. In August 1997, Parker was named director of the NASA Management Office at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in [[Pasadena, California]]. Parker retired from NASA on August 31, 2005.<ref name="nasabio" />

==Personal life==
Parker married the former Judy Woodruff of [[San Marino, California|San Marino]], [[California]]. They have five children and nine grandchildren. Parker resides with his wife in [[La Cañada Flintridge, California]].

==Honors and memberships==
Parker is a member of the [[American Astronomical Society]] and of the [[International Astronomical Union]]. He was awarded the [[NASA Exceptional Scientific Achievement Medal]] (1973) and the [[NASA Outstanding Leadership Medal]] (1974).<ref name="nasabio" />

==Media==

In the 1998 miniseries ''[[From the Earth to the Moon (miniseries)|From the Earth to the Moon]]'', Parker was portrayed by [[Chris Ellis (actor)|Chris Ellis]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0120570/fullcredits?ref_=tt_cl_sm#cast|title=From the Earth to the Moon: Full Cast and Crew|publisher=IMDB|access-date=January 4, 2018}}</ref>
